  </svg>
explanation:
R=(V² / P)=(12² / 24)=6,Ω



P'=(6² / 6)=6,W


Halving the voltage reduces power to one-quarter when resistance remains constant. Option B incorrectly assumes power is directly proportional to voltage.

title: Conventional Current Versus Electron Flow
question: A metallic wire connects the negative terminal and the positive terminal of an ideal cell in a closed circuit. The wire contains mobile electrons. Which statement correctly describes the direction of conventional current and electron drift in the external metallic wire?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 110" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M35 25 H285 V80 H35 V25"/><path d="M35 25 V43 M25 30 H45 M29 38 H41"/></g>
    <g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="18" y="60">Cell</text><text x="160" y="18">Conventional current →</text><text x="160" y="101">Electron flow ←</text></g>
    <g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><path d="M90 48 H225 M215 42 L225 48 L215 54"/><path d="M225 66 H90 M100 60 L90 66 L100 72"/></g>
  </svg>

options.text: Both move from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
Conventional current moves from negative to positive, while electrons move from positive to negative.
Both move from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
Conventional current moves from positive to negative, while electrons drift from negative to positive.

explanation: Conventional current is defined in the direction positive charges would move, from the positive terminal to the negative terminal through the external circuit. Electrons in a metal drift in the opposite direction. Option B reverses both directions.

title: Heating Effect of Current
question: Two heating elements X and Y, each of resistance 10,Ω, are separately connected to the same ideal 20,V source. Element X operates for 60,s, while element Y operates for 120,s. What is the ratio of heat produced by Y to that produced by X?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M35 25 H105 M145 25 H285 V60 H35 V25"/><rect x="105" y="15" width="40" height="20"/><path d="M35 60 V80 H105 M145 80 H285 V60"/><rect x="105" y="70" width="40" height="20"/><path d="M35 25 V42 M25 30 H45 M29 38 H41"/></g>
    <g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="125" y="8">X: 10 Ω</text><text x="125" y="64">Y: 10 Ω</text><text x="18" y="56">20 V</text><text x="220" y="18">60 s</text><text x="220" y="73">120 s</text><text x="160" y="113">Same voltage and resistance</text></g>
  </svg>
explanation:
Joule's law gives H=I^2Rt. Since the resistance and supply voltage are identical, the current is identical. Therefore, heat is directly proportional to time:


(H_Y / H_X)=(120 / 60)=2


The ratio is 2:1. Option C incorrectly squares the time ratio; Joule's law involves the square of current, not the square of time.

title: Series Circuit: Current and Potential Difference
question: A 12 V ideal battery is connected in series with a 2,Ω resistor, an ideal ammeter A, and a 4,Ω resistor. If the ammeter reads 2,A, what is the potential difference across the 4,Ω resistor and the total power supplied by the battery, respectively?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M45 45 H90 M120 45 H155 M185 45 H275 V112 H45 V45" /><rect x="90" y="35" width="30" height="20" /><circle cx="170" cy="45" r="15" /><rect x="125" y="102" width="65" height="20" /><path d="M45 58 V78 M35 64 H55 M39 72 H51" /></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="105" y="26">2 Ω</text><text x="170" y="49">A</text><text x="157" y="96">4 Ω</text><text x="18" y="91">12 V</text><text x="160" y="141">Series circuit</text></g></svg>
explanation:
1. The voltage across the 4,Ω resistor is V=IR=2×4=8,V.
2. Total power supplied by the ideal battery is P=VI=12×2=24,W.
3. The tempting error is to calculate power using only the voltage across the 4,Ω resistor. That gives 16,W, which is the power dissipated in that resistor alone, not the total power supplied.

title: Parallel Circuit: Branch Current and Voltmeter Reading
question: A 12,V ideal battery supplies two parallel branches containing 6,Ω and 3,Ω resistors. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the 6,Ω resistor. Which pair gives the current through the 3,Ω resistor and the ideal voltmeter reading?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M48 35 H100 M140 35 H272 V125 H48 V35 M48 80 H100 M140 80 H272" /><rect x="100" y="25" width="40" height="20" /><rect x="100" y="70" width="40" height="20" /><path d="M100 25 V10 H140 V25" /><circle cx="120" cy="10" r="0" /><path d="M48 35 V58 M38 43 H58 M42 51 H54" /><circle cx="120" cy="10" r="0" /></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="18"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="20"> </text><text x="120" y="40">6 Ω</text><text x="120" y="85">3 Ω</text><text x="20" y="30">12 V</text><text x="190" y="28">V across 6 Ω</text><text x="190" y="148">Parallel branches</text></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"><path d="M155 25 H166 V45 H155 M155 70 H166 V90 H155" /></g></svg>
explanation:
1. In parallel, each resistor has the full battery voltage: 12,V.
2. Current through 3,Ω: I=12/3=4,A.
3. The voltmeter reads 12,V, because it is connected across the 6,Ω resistor, which shares the same two nodes as the battery.
4. Option D incorrectly assumes that voltage divides between parallel branches.

title: Ammeter Connected in the Wrong Position
question: A 6,V ideal battery is connected to a 3,Ω resistor. An ideal ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across the resistor. What is the most accurate prediction for this idealised circuit?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 300 135" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M40 25 H120 M160 25 H260 V105 H40 V25" /><rect x="120" y="15" width="40" height="20" /><circle cx="140" cy="75" r="17" /><path d="M120 25 V75 H123 M157 75 H260 V25 M120 75 H123 M157 75 H160" /><path d="M40 25 V45 M30 32 H50 M34 40 H46" /></g><g fill="currentColor" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="140" y="8">3 Ω</text><text x="140" y="79">A</text><text x="18" y="65">6 V</text><text x="150" y="126">Ammeter shunts the resistor</text></g></svg>

options.text: The ammeter reads 2,A, as if it were in series.
The ammeter reads zero because the resistor is bypassed.
The ammeter reads 6,A, because its resistance is zero and it short-circuits the resistor.
The ammeter reads 0.5,A, because the resistor limits the current.

explanation:
1. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
2. Connected directly across the resistor, it provides a zero-resistance path between the resistor's terminals.
3. The resistor is short-circuited, and the ideal battery drives current through the zero-resistance path without a finite value in this ideal model.
4. Strictly, the current is **unbounded/undefined in the ideal model**, not 6,A. Therefore, the numerical options contain a trap: no finite current can be calculated without additional resistance.

**Correction to the options:** The scientifically correct answer is that the ideal model predicts an undefined, unbounded short-circuit current. None of the four numerical options is correct. This is precisely why an ideal ammeter must never be connected in parallel with a source or component.
